html:
The 1999 Izmit earthquake struck northwest Turkey at 3:02 in the morning on 17 August 1999, with a magnitude of 7.6. It killed more than 17,000 people by official count, and probably more, and left hundreds of thousands homeless.

The quake broke the North Anatolian Fault along about 150 km near the industrial city of Izmit, some 100 km east of Istanbul. It was one of a chain of big quakes that had moved west along the fault since the 1939 Erzincan earthquake.

Most of the dead were crushed in concrete apartment blocks that collapsed, while older and better-built buildings nearby stood. Investigations found weak concrete, missing steel and illegal extra floors, with builders and officials who looked the other way. The Tüpraş oil refinery burned for days.

Anger at the slow government response helped bring political change. Greek rescuers came to help, and when Athens was hit by a quake weeks later, Turkish teams went there; the two old rivals warmed. Turkey brought in compulsory earthquake insurance and stricter codes, but weak enforcement showed again in the 2023 earthquakes.
